docs.title: rprtr258/cli
docs.text:
A command line argument parser for Go where a parser is an ordinary Parser[T] value, composed from small building blocks with generics — so option types and validation are checked by the Go compiler, not by reflection at runtime. The parser you build drives everything: argument parsing, --help output, shell completion and even manpage rendering — you declare the command line once.

  • Type-safe. Parsers are generic Parser[T] values; composition is checked at compile time, no struct-tag reflection required.
  • One source of truth. --help text, bash/zsh/fish/elvish completion and roff manpages are all generated from the same parser definition.
  • One dependency. Just github.com/rprtr258/fun; everything else is stdlib.
  • Fast. ~1 µs and a handful of allocations to parse a 3-flag command — negligible for a once-per-process task.
  • Two declaration styles. Combinator builders or cli struct tags via Construct — same runtime underneath.
type Config struct {
    Verbose cli.Count `cli:"short=v,long=verbose"`
    Speed   float64   `cli:"long=speed,metavar=SPEED,default=42"`
    Files   []string
}

conf := cli.Construct[Config]().ToOptions().Run(os.Args)

$ app -vv --speed 3.14 a.txt b.txt
{2 3.14 [a.txt b.txt]}

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Requires Go 1.27 or newer.

go get github.com/rprtr258/cli

docs.title: Combinator declaration
docs.text:
A parser is assembled from small building blocks, composed into larger parsers, and finally run against the command line. The result is a regular Go value — the library either produces it or prints a message describing the problem (missing argument, validation failure, --help request, etc).

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "os"

    "github.com/rprtr258/cli"
)

type Rectangle struct {
    Width, Height int
}

const invalidSize = "Sides of a rectangle must be 1..20 units long"

var rectangle cli.Parser[Rectangle] = cli.Map2(
    cli.Long("width").
        Help("Width of the rectangle").
        Argument("PX", cli.ParseInt).
        Guard(func(x int) bool { return 1 <= x && x <= 20 }, invalidSize),
    cli.Long("height").
        Help("Height of the rectangle").
        Argument("PX", cli.ParseInt).
        Guard(func(x int) bool { return 1 <= x && x <= 20 }, invalidSize),
    func(w, h int) Rectangle {
        return Rectangle{Width: w, Height: h}
    }).
    Guard(func(r Rectangle) bool { return r.Width*r.Height <= 200 }, "Area of a rectangle must not exceed 200 units square")

func main() {
    rect := rectangle.ToOptions().Run(os.Args)
    fmt.Println(rect)
}

$ app --width 10 --height 5
{10 5}
$ app --width 0
parseError: `0`: Sides of a rectangle must be 1..20 units long

The declaration is fully checked by the compiler: Map2 only accepts parsers of the types the combining function expects, and Guard reuses the same value type, so mistakes surface at build time.

When the result is a plain struct, MapStruct2[T]–MapStruct6[T] drop the combining function and fill T's fields from the parser results in declaration order:

var rectangle cli.Parser[Rectangle] = cli.MapStruct2[Rectangle](width, height)

Field types are checked against the parser result types when MapStruct is called, panicking on a mismatch. See struct-based declaration for the tag-driven alternative.

docs.title: Shell completion
docs.text:
Completion for bash, zsh, fish and elvish shells is generated from the parser declaration. Pass a shell name to get a completion script:

import "github.com/rprtr258/cli"

bashCompletion := cli.CompleteBash(myParser)
zshCompletion := cli.CompleteZsh(myParser)
fishCompletion := cli.CompleteFish(myParser)
elvishCompletion := cli.CompleteElvish(myParser)

Completion is generated from the same source of truth as --help, so new flags appear in the shell as soon as they exist in the parser — nothing to keep in sync by hand.

docs.title: Where to go next

docs.title: Composing parsers
docs.text:
Composition combines parsers of different types into one:

Composer Signature Map2(f) two parsers, (T, U) -> V Map3(f) three parsers, (T, U, S) -> V Map4(f) four parsers, (T, U, S, R) -> V MapStruct2[T]-MapStruct6[T] like Map2-Map6, but fill the fields of T from the parser results in declaration order Sequence(parsers...) any parsers, []any -> V

Use Map2–Map4 when the shape is known — they stay fully type-checked. Use Sequence for arbitrary many pieces when the result can be assembled from any values.

Both styles coexist with struct-based declaration: build pieces with combinators, then feed them into a struct or combine into one Parser[T].

docs.title: Where to go next

docs.title: Ways to consume data
docs.text:
Builder Consumes Produces Short('f') / Long("flag") / Env("VAR") - NamedArg to build on NamedArg.Switch -f / --flag Parser[bool] NamedArg.Flag -f / --flag Parser[T], one of two values NamedArg.ReqFlag -f (required) Parser[T] NamedArg.Argument -f foo, --flag=bar Parser[T] NamedArg.Map --flag=KEY:VALUE, repeatable Parser[map[K]V] Positional a free-standing value Parser[T] Any any unconsumed item Parser[T] OptionParser.Command("cmd") a subcommand ParseCommand[T], an independent subparser

NamedArg.Argument and Positional take a func(string) (T, error) to convert the raw text. Ready-made adapters for common types are provided: ParseString, ParseInt, ParseInt32, ParseUint, ParseFloat, ParseBool, ParseDuration.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The examples directory in the repo contains runnable programs covering most of the API — each file is adapted from a clap.rs example with the same name. A few entry points:

  • basic.go — minimal flag with help.
  • rectangle.go — two validated arguments composed with Map2 and Guard.
  • construct_struct.go — struct-based declaration.
  • git.go — subcommands.
  • env_variable.go — fallback to environment variables.
  • customize_help.go — appname, description, copyright, version.
  • with_examples.go — documented usage examples, validated against the parser.

Run any of them from the repo root:

go run ./examples/rectangle --width 10 --height 5

docs.title: Error messages
docs.text:
Missing arguments and failed Guard checks produce helpful errors that list all valid ways to use the parser:

$ app --user
parseError: missing required argument: --user=USER
$ app --width 0
parseError: `0`: Sides of a rectangle must be 1..20 units long

docs.title: Customizing help output
docs.text:
Use these methods on OptionParser before .Run:

Method Effect Description(...) Program description at the top of help Appname(...) Program name instead of os.Args[0] Version(...) Print --version output and exit Copyright(...) Copyright header at the top of help Example(descr, command) Documented usage example in help and manpage

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Example(descr, command) documents a usage example. Examples are shown in the Examples: section of the --help output and in the EXAMPLES section of rendered manpages:

parser.ToOptions().
    Description("Copy files and directories").
    Example("Copy a file to a directory", "file.txt backup/").
    Example("Copy a directory recursively", "--recursive src/ dst/")

$ app --help
Copy files and directories

Usage: app [-r] SRC DST

<skip>

Examples:
    Copy a file to a directory  $ app file.txt backup/
    Copy a directory recursively  $ app --recursive src/ dst/

The command line is written relative to the parser the example is declared on: without the program name and, for subcommands, without the command name — the program name and command path are prepended automatically when rendering.

Examples are validated whenever the parser runs: the command line is tokenized (shell-style, quotes are supported) and parsed with the parser the example is declared on. If an example stops parsing after a parser change, Run, RunE and CheckInvariants panic with a cli usage BUG message naming the stale example, so the documentation cannot silently disagree with the parser. This also executes the example converters, so example command lines must not have side effects.

docs.title: Man pages
docs.text: The roff package renders manpage source from the same declaration the program runs on, so the manpage can never disagree with the actual behavior. Declared examples are rendered into the EXAMPLES section. Export to Markdown is planned (see the roadmap comment in doc.go) but not implemented yet.

docs.title: Help formatting
docs.text: --help prints the usage line, options with their types, metavariables, defaults and environment fallbacks. The exact layout is covered by golden tests in the repo.

docs.title: Where to go next

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
A parser runs against os.Args:

conf := parser.ToOptions().Run(os.Args)

Run either returns the parsed value or terminates the process: it prints the error (or --help / --version output) and exits with an appropriate code. For programs that want to handle errors themselves, Parse returns the value or an error instead of exiting.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Parsers are ordinary values, so tests feed os.Args-shaped slices into the parser and assert on the result — no subprocesses or golden files are required:

func TestRectangle(t *testing.T) {
    rect, err := rectangle.Parse([]string{"--width", "10", "--height", "5"})
    require.NoError(t, err)
    require.Equal(t, Rectangle{Width: 10, Height: 5}, rect)
}

Help output is verified with golden files in the repo, and the CI runs the lint and test suites on every push to master and on pull requests.

CheckInvariants also validates declared usage examples: every example command line must parse with the parser it is declared on, otherwise it panics with a cli usage BUG message naming the stale example (see Help and UX).

docs.title: Struct-based declaration
docs.text:
Struct-based declaration lets you describe the command line as a plain Go struct. Field types choose the consumers:

Field type Meaning bool a switch primitives an argument (a positional if the field has no name) []E zero or more values []*E zero or more values, elements are pointers *E optional value, nil when absent cli.Opt[E] optional value cli.Count number of repeats map[K]V repeated KEY:VALUE named argument accumulating into a map; entries split at the first colon struct with command=NAME subcommand: inner fields are parsed only when the command name is given struct with group=NAME option group: inner fields parse as usual options but are rendered in help under their own section

Non-trivial options — short names, help text, env fallbacks, defaults — go into the cli struct tag:

type Out struct {
    Debug bool   `cli:"short=d,long=debug,help='Activate debug mode'"`
    Home  string `cli:"long=home,env=HOME"`
    Tags  map[string]string `cli:"long=tag,help='Tags as KEY:VALUE'"`
    Pet   string `cli:"long=pet,choice=cat,choice=dog"`
    HideMe string `cli:"long=hide-me,hidden"`
}

Supported tag keys:

Tag Meaning short=a short name, one character; repeatable for hidden aliases long=name long name; repeatable for hidden aliases metavar=X placeholder shown in help, defaults to the uppercased field name help=... help message env=VAR environment variable fallback default=v value used when the field is absent; not valid for bool, slice, pointer, cli.Opt[E] and cli.Count; on map fields repeatable, each entry is key:value positional forces positional parsing; fields without short/long/env are positional automatically command=NAME struct field is a subcommand with the given name alias=A hidden long alias for a command field, repeatable group=NAME struct field options are rendered in help under their own section hidden parse the field but omit it from help and completion choice=V allowed argument values, repeatable; a value not listed fails parsing

Named fields are parsed first, then command fields, then positionals, regardless of declaration order. A nested struct field requires either command= or group= — a plain nested struct panics.

Turn a struct into a parser with Construct:

conf := cli.Construct[Config]().ToOptions().Run(os.Args)

This is the same runtime as the combinator declaration, just with the layout written as types and tags instead of builder calls.

docs.title: Transforming parsers
docs.text:
Once a consumer produces a Parser[T], the chain below changes how it is parsed. The return type in brackets matters: some transformers only exist on parsers of some types, e.g. Some only makes sense on repeatable things and Def is not applicable to switches, which are always present.

Transformer Signature What it does Guard Parser[T] -> Parser[T] Check the parsed value is valid: .Guard(func(t T) bool, "message") Def Parser[T] -> Parser[T] Fall back when missing: .Def(x) Map Parser[T] -> Parser[U] Pure transform of the value: .Map(func(t T) U) Map2 (Parser[T], Parser[U]) -> Parser[V] Pure transform of two parsers MapStruct2-MapStruct6 (Parser[T], Parser[U], ...) -> Parser[V] Fill V's fields from the parser results in declaration order Some Parser[T] -> Parser[[]T] One or more values Many Parser[T] -> Parser[[]T] Zero or more values Optional Parser[T] -> Parser[Opt[T]] Zero or one value Count Parser[T] -> Parser[int] Number of repeats, ignores the values DefaultsTo Parser[T] -> Parser[Ext[T]] Tells which values were explicitly passed and which are default SetEnv Parser[T] -> Parser[T] Take the value from the given environment variable if the command line does not provide it

Missing required arguments and failed Guards produce user-readable errors automatically, listing all valid ways to use the parser.
